goals: Explain the purpose of comparative and common-size statements as tools of financial statement analysis

slides.heading: Financial Statement Analysis: Comparative Statements
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what **comparative** and **common-size** statements are for, why they matter, where they fall short, and how to prepare **comparative statements** of one firm over two years and of two firms in one year. Every company and figure in this chapter is imagined.

Two tools: comparative and common-size
Significance and limitations
Comparative Statement of Profit and Loss
Comparative Balance Sheet
Inter-firm comparison

visual.alt: Route map of Part one: why statements are analysed, the two tools of this chapter, their significance and limitations, the comparative statement of profit and loss, the comparative balance sheet, and comparison between two firms
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Financial statements tell us what happened in one year. Analysis asks what the figures mean: is the business growing, are its costs under control, is it safe to lend to it? In this part we meet two tools of analysis and prepare comparative statements. Our running company is Shivneri Fruit Pulp of Narayangaon, a maker of mango and guava pulp.

slides.heading: Tools of financial statement analysis
slides.body_md: Your syllabus pairs **comparative** and **common-size** statements in this chapter; the cash flow statement and ratios follow.

rows: The same items for two or more years (or two firms) side by side, with the absolute and percentage change
Every item as a percentage of a common base of the same statement
Inflows and outflows of cash by activity
One figure related to another, such as current assets to current liabilities

visual.alt: Table of the tools of financial statement analysis: comparative statements show change over years or between firms, which is horizontal analysis; common-size statements show each item as a percentage of a base, which is vertical analysis; the cash flow statement and ratio analysis follow in the next chapters
visual.caption: This chapter covers the first two tools.

slides.narration: Analysts use several tools. Comparative statements put two years, or two firms, side by side and show how far each item has changed. Common-size statements turn every item into a share of a common base. The cash flow statement and ratio analysis are the next two chapters of the same section of your paper.

slides.heading: Horizontal and vertical analysis
slides.body_md: Comparative statements read **across** the years; common-size statements read **down** one statement.

rows: How far has each item moved?
What share of the base is each item?
The same item in the earlier year
Revenue from operations, or the balance sheet total

visual.alt: Table contrasting horizontal and vertical analysis: horizontal analysis studies how each item moved across years with the earlier year as base, using comparative statements; vertical analysis studies the share of each item in a base of the same year, using common-size statements

slides.narration: Horizontal analysis follows one item across the years, so it is also called dynamic analysis. Its percentages are worked on the earlier year. Vertical analysis studies the make-up of one statement, so it is called static analysis, and its percentages are worked on a base of the same year, such as revenue from operations or the balance sheet total.

slides.heading: Significance: who uses them and why
bullets: They show the **trend** and the **speed** of change.
They point to **strengths and weak spots** that need action.
Common-size figures make firms of **different sizes** comparable.

rows: Which costs grow faster than revenue; where control and planning are needed
Whether profit and the profit margin are rising
Changes in current assets and liabilities (short-term) and in borrowings and owners’ funds (long-term)
Whether the company can pay its trade payables on time
How the company compares with others of different size (inter-firm)

visual.alt: Table of readers and what the statements tell them: management sees which costs outgrow revenue, shareholders see profit and margin, lenders see short-term and long-term solvency, suppliers see the ability to pay, and analysts compare firms of different sizes

slides.narration: Comparative and common-size statements matter because they turn a mass of figures into a few clear signals. Management sees which costs outgrow revenue. Shareholders see whether the margin is rising. Banks and suppliers judge whether they will be paid. Analysts compare a firm with rivals of a very different size.

slides.heading: Limitations
slides.body_md: The statements show **what** changed; the analyst must still find out **why**.

rows: They describe the past; decisions are about the future
A rise in rupees may be only inflation
Skill, morale, reputation and competition have no rupee figure
Firms using different methods are not strictly comparable
Figures can be made to look better on the balance sheet date
A change shows where to look, not why it happened

visual.alt: Table of six limitations: figures are historical, price changes are ignored, qualitative factors are left out, accounting policies differ between firms, figures can be window dressed, and the statements show symptoms rather than causes

slides.narration: These tools have limits. They work on past figures, which are not adjusted for changes in prices. They leave out things that have no rupee value, such as the skill of the staff. Different accounting policies make firms hard to compare, figures can be window dressed, and a change only tells the analyst where to look.

slides.heading: Quick check: which statement shows what?
slides.body_md: Match each statement with what it shows.
slides.narration: Ask of each statement whether it measures change or measures shares of a base, and whether it compares years or firms.

slides.heading: The comparative statement: format and formulas
slides.body_md: Absolute change = later − earlier.  Percentage change = absolute change ÷ earlier × 100.

rows: The heads and sub-heads in Schedule III order (no notes column)
Later year − earlier year; a decrease in brackets
Absolute change ÷ earlier year × 100, to two decimals; a dash if the earlier figure is nil

visual.alt: Table of the five columns of a comparative statement: particulars in schedule order, the earlier year as the base, the later year, the absolute change as later minus earlier, and the percentage change as absolute change divided by the earlier year times one hundred, rounded to two decimals
visual.caption: Rounding rule: every percentage is rounded to two decimal places, a third decimal of 5 or more raising the second decimal (in size).

slides.narration: A comparative statement has five columns: the particulars, the earlier year, the later year, the absolute change and the percentage change. The absolute change is the later figure minus the earlier one. The percentage change divides that change by the earlier figure and multiplies by one hundred. Round every percentage to two decimals and show a fall in brackets.

slides.body_md: Fill in the missing word.
slides.narration: Recall which year’s figure the absolute change is divided by.

slides.heading: Reading a comparative statement
slides.body_md: Always compare the growth of each cost with the growth of **revenue**.

rows: Profit growing more slowly than sales; costs need control
Profit growing faster than sales (some costs are fixed)
More borrowing or a higher rate of interest
Inventories or receivables rising faster than revenue
Slow-moving stock or slow collection from customers
Assets growing with owners’ funds, borrowings cut

visual.alt: Table on reading a comparative statement: expenses outgrowing revenue squeezes profit; revenue outgrowing expenses widens it; sharply rising finance costs point to more borrowing; stock or receivables outgrowing revenue point to slow sales or collection; growth financed by owners with borrowings cut is safer

slides.narration: A comparative statement is read by comparing rates of change. If expenses grow faster than revenue, profit grows more slowly than sales. Sharply rising finance costs point to more borrowing. Stock or receivables growing faster than sales point to slow-moving goods or slow collection. Growth financed by owners, with borrowings cut, makes a business safer.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: Shivneri’s Comparative Balance Sheet
slides.body_md: Both totals rise by ₹6,40,000, that is **15.24%**.

rows: **(a) Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets**

visual.alt: Comparative balance sheet of Shivneri: total rupees forty-two lakh rising to rupees forty-eight lakh forty thousand, a change of fifteen point two four per cent on both sides
visual.caption: Comparative Balance Sheet of Shivneri Fruit Pulp Ltd (imagined) as at 31 March 2025 and 31 March 2026.

slides.narration: Each sub-head of the two balance sheets is set side by side in Schedule Three order. Reserves rose by thirty-three point three three per cent, long-term borrowings fell by twenty per cent and cash fell by six point six seven per cent. Both totals rise by rupees six lakh forty thousand: the change on one side must equal the change on the other.

slides.heading: Worked example 2 (continued): reading the heads
bullets: Owners' funds up **26.92%**; long-term debt down **20.00%**: growth was financed by owners.
Non-current assets up **15.33%**: new pulping machinery.
Current liabilities (23.33%) grew faster than current assets (15.00%): watch liquidity.

visual.alt: Head totals of Shivneri: shareholders funds up twenty-six point nine two per cent, non-current liabilities down twenty per cent, current liabilities up twenty-three point three three per cent, non-current assets up fifteen point three three per cent and current assets up fifteen per cent
visual.caption: Each head is added from its sub-heads first; its percentage is worked on its own earlier total.

slides.narration: Adding the sub-heads gives the major heads. Shareholders funds grew by twenty-six point nine two per cent while long-term borrowings were cut, so the company is less dependent on debt. But current liabilities grew faster than current assets, and cash fell, so its short-term position needs watching.

slides.heading: Quick check: a fall in cash
slides.body_md: True or false?
slides.narration: Work out the change, divide it by the earlier figure, and remember how a decrease is shown.

slides.heading: Intra-firm and inter-firm comparison
slides.body_md: In an inter-firm statement the **base firm** takes the place of the earlier year.

rows: The period (same firm, two or more years)
The firm (same period, two or more firms)
Absolute change; % change on the earlier year
Difference; % difference on the base firm
Is the firm doing better than last year?
Is the firm doing better than its rival?

visual.alt: Table contrasting intra-firm and inter-firm comparison: intra-firm keeps the firm and changes the year, with percentages on the earlier year; inter-firm keeps the year and changes the firm, with percentages on the base firm

slides.narration: Comparing a firm with its own past is intra-firm comparison. Comparing two firms for the same year is inter-firm comparison. The layout is the same, but the columns are the two firms, and the differences are worked on the firm chosen as the base.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: two brassware makers
slides.body_md: Jaigarh Brassware Ltd (base) and Kumbhalgarh Brassware Ltd, both imagined, for 2025-26. Tax 25% of profit before tax.

rows: IV. Less: Tax (25% of profit before tax)

visual.alt: Inter-firm comparative statement: Kumbhalgarh's revenue is twenty-five per cent higher than Jaigarh's, its total expenses thirty-two point eight one per cent higher, and its profit after tax six point two five per cent lower
visual.caption: Inter-firm Comparative Statement of Profit and Loss of Jaigarh Brassware Ltd (base) and Kumbhalgarh Brassware Ltd (both imagined), year ended 31 March 2026. Tax 25% for both.

slides.narration: Kumbhalgarh sells twenty-five per cent more than Jaigarh, yet earns six point two five per cent less profit after tax. Its materials cost thirty-five point four two per cent more and its other expenses are much higher, so its total expenses are thirty-two point eight one per cent above Jaigarh's. Bigger is not always more profitable.

slides.heading: Quick check: a percentage change
slides.body_md: Work it out.
slides.narration: Subtract the earlier figure from the later one, then divide by the earlier figure and multiply by one hundred.

slides.heading: Special cases
slides.body_md: A head or total gets its **own** percentage, worked on its own earlier total.

rows: Worked on its own earlier total, never an average of the line percentages
Two decimals; 0.005 rounds up in size

visual.alt: Table of special cases: a fall is shown in brackets in both columns; an unchanged item shows zero; when the earlier figure is nil only the rupee change is shown and the percentage is a dash; a total has its own percentage on its own earlier total; percentages are rounded to two decimals

slides.narration: A few cases need care. A fall is shown in brackets in both change columns. An unchanged item shows zero. When the earlier figure is nil there is nothing to divide by, so only the rupee change is shown. And never average the percentages of the lines to get the percentage of a total.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Two years (or firms) side by side with absolute and percentage change
Later − earlier (or other firm − base firm)
Absolute change ÷ earlier year (or base firm) × 100, two decimals
Both totals change by the same amount and percentage
Trend, strengths and weaknesses, solvency, comparison with rivals
Historical, price changes ignored, qualitative factors left out, policies differ

visual.alt: Summary table of Part one: the comparative statement, the formulas for absolute and percentage change, the balance sheet check, and the significance and limitations of the tool

slides.narration: To sum up: comparative statements set two years, or two firms, side by side. The absolute change is later minus earlier, and the percentage change divides it by the earlier figure. Both balance sheet totals change by the same amount. The statements show trends and weak spots, but they rest on past, unadjusted figures and leave out qualitative factors.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Complete **both years** (totals, profit before tax, tax, profit after tax) before the change columns.
Divide by the **earlier year** (or the base firm), never by the later year.
Show decreases in **brackets** in both change columns; a dash when the earlier figure is nil.
Round to **two decimals** and say so; work each total’s percentage on that total.
Check that both balance sheet totals change by the **same** amount and percentage.
slides.narration: In the exam, finish both years before working out any change. Always divide by the earlier year or the base firm. Put decreases in brackets in both change columns. Round to two decimals and state the rule. Work out the percentage of every total on that total, and check that both sides of a balance sheet change by the same amount.

slides.narration: A rupee figure on its own says little about structure. Is a materials bill of rupees twenty-nine lakh large? Only when we see what share of revenue it takes. In this part we turn statements into shares of one hundred. Our running company is Panhala Jaggery of Kodoli, which crushes sugarcane into jaggery blocks and powder.

slides.heading: Meaning and the base
slides.body_md: Revenue from operations = **100** for profit and loss; the balance sheet total = **100** for each part of the balance sheet.

rows: Common-size Statement of Profit and Loss
Revenue from operations of that year
Item ÷ revenue from operations × 100 (other income too, so total income may exceed 100)
Total of the balance sheet on that date
Item ÷ total × 100; each part (equity and liabilities, assets) adds to 100

visual.alt: Table of the base for each common-size statement: revenue from operations for the statement of profit and loss, where other income is also divided by revenue so total income may exceed one hundred; the balance sheet total for the balance sheet, where each part adds to one hundred

slides.narration: A common-size statement shows every item as a percentage of a common base of the same statement. In the statement of profit and loss, revenue from operations is the base, so even other income is divided by it, and total income can exceed one hundred. In the balance sheet, the total is the base, and each part adds to one hundred.

slides.heading: Format of a common-size statement
slides.body_md: Each year is divided by **its own** base.

rows: Heads and sub-heads in Schedule III order
Each amount ÷ the base of its own year × 100, two decimals

visual.alt: Table of the columns of a common-size statement: particulars in schedule order, the rupee amounts of both years, and each amount as a percentage of its own year base, to two decimals
visual.caption: The base of each year is that year’s own revenue or total; never divide a later-year figure by an earlier-year base.

slides.narration: The usual layout shows the rupee amounts of both years and then the percentages of both years. Each year is divided by its own revenue or its own total. Percentages are rounded to two decimals. The heads and sub-heads stay in Schedule Three order.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: Panhala’s common-size Statement of Profit and Loss

sections.heading: 1. Financial statement analysis and its tools
sections.body_md:
**Financial statement analysis** is the study of the Statement of Profit and Loss and the Balance Sheet to judge a company's profitability, solvency and efficiency, by comparing items over time, with other firms, and with each other.

**Tools:** comparative statements and common-size statements (this chapter), the cash flow statement (Chapter 11) and ratio analysis (Chapter 12).

- **Horizontal (dynamic) analysis:** the same item across two or more periods; tool: comparative statements.
- **Vertical (static) analysis:** each item against a base of the same period; tool: common-size statements.

*Not in the ISC 2027 syllabus:* notes to accounts. The statements in this chapter are prepared at head and sub-head level only, without a Note No. column.

key_terms.definition_md: Studying the financial statements, by comparison over time, between firms and between items, to judge profitability, solvency and efficiency.
Analysis of the change in each item over two or more periods; also called dynamic analysis.
Analysis of each item as a share of a base of the same period; also called static analysis.

rows: The same items for two or more years (or two firms) side by side, with the absolute and percentage change
Every item as a percentage of a common base of the same statement
Inflows and outflows of cash by activity
One figure related to another, such as current assets to current liabilities

visual.caption: This chapter covers the first two tools.

rows: How far has each item moved?
What share of the base is each item?
The same item in the earlier year
Revenue from operations, or the balance sheet total

visuals.alt: Table contrasting horizontal and vertical analysis: horizontal analysis studies how each item moved across years with the earlier year as base, using comparative statements; vertical analysis studies the share of each item in a base of the same year, using common-size statements

sections.heading: 2. Significance and limitations
sections.body_md:
**Significance**
1. Show the **trend** of revenue, costs, profit, assets and liabilities, and the speed of each change.
2. Point to **strengths and weaknesses** (costs outgrowing revenue, rising borrowing, slow-moving stock) so management can act.
3. Help judge **profitability and solvency** for shareholders, lenders and suppliers.
4. Make **inter-firm comparison** possible; common-size figures remove the effect of size.
5. Support **planning and forecasting**.

**Limitations**
1. Based on **historical** figures; decisions concern the future.
2. **Price-level changes** are ignored; a rise in rupees may be inflation.
3. **Qualitative factors** (management, labour relations, competition) are left out.
4. Different **accounting policies** make firms hard to compare.
5. Figures may be **window-dressed**.
6. They show **symptoms, not causes**; interpretation needs judgement. Common-size statements have no accepted standard share for each item.

key_terms.definition_md: Comparing the same firm over two or more periods.
Comparing two or more firms for the same period.
Presenting the financial position as better than it is on the balance sheet date.

rows: Which costs grow faster than revenue; where control and planning are needed
Whether profit and the profit margin are rising
Changes in current assets and liabilities (short-term) and in borrowings and owners’ funds (long-term)
Whether the company can pay its trade payables on time
How the company compares with others of different size (inter-firm)

rows: They describe the past; decisions are about the future
A rise in rupees may be only inflation
Skill, morale, reputation and competition have no rupee figure
Firms using different methods are not strictly comparable
Figures can be made to look better on the balance sheet date
A change shows where to look, not why it happened

sections.heading: 3. Comparative statements: format and formulas
sections.body_md:
A **comparative statement** shows the Statement of Profit and Loss or the Balance Sheet of two (or more) years, or of two firms, side by side, with the change in each item.

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| Particulars | Heads and sub-heads in Schedule III order |
| Earlier year (₹) | The base |
| Later year (₹) | |
| Absolute change (₹) | Later year − earlier year |
| Percentage change (%) | Absolute change ÷ earlier year × 100 |

**Rounding rule: every percentage is rounded to two decimal places, a third decimal of 5 or more raising the second decimal (in size).** A decrease is shown in brackets in both change columns. If the earlier figure is nil, the percentage change is shown as a dash. A total or a head gets its own percentage on its own earlier total.

key_terms.definition_md: The later-year figure minus the earlier-year figure, in rupees.

sections.heading: 8. Inter-firm common-size statements and interpretation
sections.body_md:
**Inter-firm common-size statement:** each firm's items divided by that firm's own revenue or total; the effect of size disappears, so cost structure, margins and financing can be compared.

**Sindhudurg and Vijaydurg Fish Foods (imagined):** profit after tax 15.00% against 14.25% of revenue, although Vijaydurg's rupee profit (₹11,40,000) is far larger.

**Interpreting both tools together:** a comparative statement shows how far each item moved; a common-size statement shows whether its share grew. A large percentage change on a tiny base, or a falling share that hides a rising amount, misleads when one tool is read alone.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Dividing the change by the later year (or by the other firm) instead of the earlier year (or the base firm).
- Working a total's percentage as the average of its lines' percentages.
- Forgetting brackets for decreases, or showing a percentage when the earlier figure is nil.
- In a common-size statement of profit and loss, dividing by total income instead of revenue from operations; in a balance sheet, dividing liabilities by total liabilities only.
- Dividing a later-year item by the earlier year's base.
- Leaving a common-size balance sheet part at 100.01 or 99.99 without adjusting and explaining one line.
- Judging profitability by rupee profit when firms differ in size; reading a falling share as a falling amount.

**How marks are usually awarded (SOYL chapter tests on the ISC default pattern)**
- 1 mark: objective items.
- 2 marks: two changes or two common-size shares worked out; two differences or two limitations.
- 3 marks: a short comparative or common-size statement (both years completed 1, first set of figures 1, second set 1), or interpretation of a given statement.
- 5 marks in parts, e.g. (a) 3 + (b) 2: a full statement and two observations.
- Full practice problem (8 marks): both statements for the same company plus one observation. The ISC 2027 weightage for Financial Statement Analysis in Paper I Section B is 4 marks.

**Figures in SOYL practice** are imagined; your board paper will give its own.

questions.stem_md: The accountant of Kenjalgad Spices Ltd, an imagined company, sets its balance sheets of 31 March 2025 and 31 March 2026 side by side and adds one column for the rupee change and one for the percentage change in each item. She has prepared

options.text_md: a common-size balance sheet
a comparative balance sheet
a cash flow statement
a trial balance

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a comparative balance sheet. Two dates side by side with the change in rupees and in per cent is the comparative form; a common-size statement would turn each item into a share of the total instead.

questions.stem_md: An analyst at Sudhagad Bamboo Ltd, an imagined company, reads each row of its comparative statement of profit and loss from the 2024-25 column across to the 2025-26 column to see how far the item has moved. This kind of study is known as

options.text_md: vertical (static) analysis
ratio analysis
cash flow analysis
horizontal (dynamic) analysis

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** horizontal (dynamic) analysis. Following one item over time is horizontal or dynamic analysis; relating items to a base within one year is vertical or static analysis.

questions.stem_md: The finance manager of Vasota Honey Ltd, an imagined company, works out every item of its 2025-26 Statement of Profit and Loss as a percentage of revenue from operations of the same year. This is an example of

options.text_md: vertical (static) analysis
horizontal (dynamic) analysis
trend analysis over several years
inter-firm comparison

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** vertical (static) analysis. Every item is set against a base of the same period, which is what vertical analysis means; the common-size statement is its usual tool.

questions.stem_md: Between 2024-25 and 2025-26 the revenue from operations of Rohtas Lime Works Ltd, an imagined company in Sasaram, rose by 9%, while the price of lime rose by about 8% over the same period. Read on its own, the comparative statement of profit and loss

options.text_md: shows that the company sold 9% more tonnes of lime
is wrong, because comparative statements cannot be prepared when prices change
overstates the real growth in sales, because comparative figures are not adjusted for changes in the price level
automatically removes the effect of the price rise

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** overstates the real growth in sales, because comparative figures are not adjusted for changes in the price level. Rupee figures of two years are compared as they stand; most of the 9% rise here is price, not volume, and the statement cannot tell the two apart.

questions.stem_md: Kamalgad Rice Mills Ltd charges depreciation on the straight-line method, while Rohida Rice Mills Ltd uses the written-down value method (both companies imagined). In their inter-firm common-size statements depreciation is 2.00% of revenue for one and 5.00% for the other. The analyst should conclude that

options.text_md: Rohida's machines are certainly older and less efficient
the two companies cannot be compared at all, because their sizes differ
part of the gap may come from the different depreciation methods, so the comparison must be read with care
one of the two statements must contain an arithmetical error

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** part of the gap may come from the different depreciation methods, so the comparison must be read with care. Different accepted accounting policies give different figures for the same facts, which is a standing limitation of inter-firm comparison.

questions.stem_md: A bank deciding whether to raise the cash credit limit of Hatgad Grapes Ltd, an imagined company, studies its comparative balance sheet. The lines it will watch most closely are the changes in

options.text_md: current assets and current liabilities
share capital and securities premium
property, plant and equipment and long-term borrowings only
the number of equity shares issued

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** current assets and current liabilities. A cash credit is a short-term facility, so the lender looks at short-term solvency: how current assets and current liabilities have moved.

questions.stem_md: Which question about Malhargad Bakery Ltd, an imagined company, can its comparative statement of profit and loss for 2024-25 and 2025-26 answer, but its 2025-26 statement alone cannot?

options.text_md: What was the profit after tax for 2025-26?
What was the revenue from operations in 2025-26?
How much tax was charged in 2025-26?
Did expenses grow faster than revenue from operations over the year?

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Did expenses grow faster than revenue from operations over the year? A single statement gives the levels of one year; only a second year side by side shows the direction and speed of change.

questions.stem_md: Mahipatgad Cashew Ltd has revenue of ₹50 lakh and a rival processor, Prabalgad Cashew Ltd, has revenue of ₹5 crore (both imagined). To compare what share of its revenue each spends on employees, the analyst should prepare

options.text_md: comparative balance sheets of each company for two years
common-size statements of profit and loss of the two companies
a cash flow statement of each company
a trial balance of each company

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** common-size statements of profit and loss of the two companies. Rupee amounts of a small and a large firm cannot be compared directly, but percentages of each firm’s own revenue can.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A comparative statement of profit and loss helps the directors of Tikona Brass Fittings Ltd, an imagined company, see whether costs are rising faster than revenue from operations.

**Reason (R):** A comparative statement places the figures of two years side by side and shows the absolute and percentage change in each item.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and the side-by-side change columns are exactly what let the directors compare the growth of costs with the growth of revenue, so R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The comparative statements of Orchha Handmade Paper Ltd, an imagined company, can mislead when prices have risen sharply between the two years.

**Reason (R):** Comparative and common-size statements are prepared from the published financial statements of the company.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true. A is true because historical rupee figures are not adjusted for inflation; R only says where the figures come from, which does not explain why a price rise distorts them.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Because the comparative statement of Daulatabad Paper Ltd, an imagined company, shows a 25.00% rise in revenue from operations, the company must have sold 25.00% more paper.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Revenue is price times quantity; the rise may come partly or wholly from higher prices, which the statement does not separate.

questions.stem_md: Because it follows each item of Malhargad Bakery Ltd from one year to the next, the study of its comparative statements is also called ___ analysis.
questions.solution_md: It is horizontal (dynamic) analysis, as opposed to the vertical (static) analysis of common-size statements.

questions.stem_md: Match each statement prepared by the accountant of Vasota Honey Ltd (column A) with what it shows (column B).

options.text_md: Comparative statement of profit and loss
Common-size balance sheet
Inter-firm comparative statement
Common-size statement of profit and loss

match_right.text_md: Each item as a percentage of the balance sheet total of the same date
Each item as a percentage of revenue from operations
Each income and expense of two years with its absolute and percentage change
The difference between Vasota and a rival company for the same year

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Comparative statements measure change (over time or between firms); common-size statements measure shares of a base.

questions.stem_md: A trainee at Karnala Poultry Ltd, an imagined company, asks: (a) What is a common-size statement? (b) Why is it called a tool of vertical analysis?
questions.solution_md: One mark for the meaning with both bases, one for linking "vertical" to the same-period base.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A common-size statement shows every item of a financial statement as a percentage of a common base of the same period: revenue from operations (taken as 100) in a common-size Statement of Profit and Loss, and the balance sheet total (taken as 100) in a common-size Balance Sheet. Rupee amounts are usually shown beside the percentages.

**(b)** It relates each item to a base **within the same year**, reading down the statement rather than across years, so it shows the make-up of one statement at a time. That study of the structure of a single period is called vertical (static) analysis.

marking_scheme.step: Meaning with the base for each statement

questions.stem_md: Mention two limitations of comparative and common-size statements that the directors of Orchha Handmade Paper Ltd should keep in mind before acting on them.
questions.solution_md: Any two distinct limitations, each with a line of explanation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Historical, unadjusted figures.** The statements use past book figures; a rise in rupees may be only a rise in prices, and assets bought years ago stay at old costs, so the trend can mislead.
2. **Qualitative factors are left out.** The skill of the paper makers, the loyalty of customers or a new competitor carry no rupee amount, so no percentage can show them.

*(Also accepted)* Different accounting policies make inter-firm comparison unreliable; window dressing distorts the figures; the statements show what changed, not why.

questions.stem_md: Hatgad Grapes Ltd, an imagined company, has prepared comparative statements for the first time. Give two ways in which they will help its directors.
questions.solution_md: Two uses, each tied to a decision the directors take.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **They show the trend.** The directors can see at a glance which items rose or fell and by how much, for example whether the cost of grapes and packing grew faster than revenue, and act on it.
2. **They point to strengths and weaknesses.** Large percentage changes (finance costs, inventories, trade receivables) draw attention to areas that need control, and help in planning and budgeting for the next season.

*(Also accepted)* They help judge whether profitability and solvency improved; they make inter-firm comparison possible when a rival’s figures are set beside Hatgad’s.

questions.stem_md: Explain three purposes for which the management of Raisen Soya Ltd, an imagined company, can use its comparative and common-size statements.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct purposes, each with the part of the statements that serves it.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **To study the trend of performance:** the comparative statements show how revenue, each expense and profit moved over the year, so management sees whether the soya business is growing and whether costs are under control.
2. **To understand the structure of costs and funds:** common-size statements show what share of every rupee of revenue goes to soybeans, wages, interest and other costs, and how the business is financed (owners, long-term debt, current liabilities), so imbalances stand out.
3. **To compare with other firms:** because common-size figures remove the effect of size, Raisen can set its cost shares and margin beside those of a larger or smaller processor and find where it is less efficient.

*(Also accepted)* To judge short-term and long-term solvency; to support planning, budgeting and forecasting; to locate the causes of a change in profit.

questions.stem_md: The chairman of Ghangad Tea Ltd, an imagined company, tells the board: "Our comparative statements show sales up 30.00%, so we are clearly a better company than last year." State three limitations of these statements that a director should point out to him.
questions.solution_md: Three limitations, each linked to why the 30.00% figure is not enough on its own.

answer.model_answer_md:
- **Price changes are ignored.** Tea prices may have risen; a 30.00% rise in rupees can hide a much smaller rise, or even a fall, in the quantity sold.
- **Sales alone do not show efficiency.** The statements must be read as a whole: if costs rose faster than sales, profit and its share of revenue may have fallen. A rise in one figure does not make the company better.
- **Non-money factors are left out.** The quality of the tea, the condition of the bushes, labour relations and competition do not appear in the statements, yet they decide whether the company is really stronger.

*(Also accepted)* Figures depend on accounting policies and estimates and may be window-dressed; the statements show what changed but not why; past results do not guarantee future ones.

marking_scheme.step: First limitation applied to the claim

questions.stem_md:
Suvarnadurg Fisheries Ltd, an imagined company, is preparing its first set of analysed statements.

(a) Explain the meaning of comparative statements and any two points of their significance to the company. (3 marks)
(b) State two limitations of common-size statements. (2 marks)
questions.solution_md: Part (a): meaning (1) and two points of significance (2); part (b): two limitations (2).

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a) Meaning.** Comparative statements present the Statement of Profit and Loss or the Balance Sheet of two or more periods (or of two firms) side by side, with the absolute change and the percentage change in each item, so that the direction and size of every change can be seen.

**Significance (any two).**
- They show the trend of revenue, costs and profit, so management of the fishery can see whether growth is healthy, for example whether fuel and ice costs rise faster than sales.
- They reveal changes in financial position: how far assets grew and whether they were financed by owners or by borrowing.
- *(Also accepted)* They help compare the company with rivals (inter-firm) and support planning and forecasting.

**(b) Limitations of common-size statements (any two).**
- They show only shares of a base; a falling percentage may hide a rising rupee amount, so they must be read with the rupee figures.
- There is no accepted standard share for each item, so judging whether a share is "too high" needs comparison with other years or firms; and they ignore price changes and qualitative factors.

questions.stem_md: In the comparative balance sheet of Suvarnadurg Fisheries Ltd, an imagined company, the percentage change in trade payables is found by dividing the absolute change by

options.text_md: the trade payables on 31 March 2025, the earlier date
the trade payables on 31 March 2026, the later date
the balance sheet total on 31 March 2026
the revenue from operations of 2025-26

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the trade payables on 31 March 2025, the earlier date. Percentage change = absolute change ÷ earlier-year amount × 100: the earlier figure is the base.

questions.stem_md: Inventories of Kulang Seeds Ltd, an imagined company, were ₹2,40,000 on 31 March 2025 and ₹3,00,000 on 31 March 2026. In its comparative balance sheet, the percentage change in inventories is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 25.00%. Change = 3,00,000 − 2,40,000 = 60,000; 60,000 ÷ 2,40,000 × 100 = 25.00%. Dividing by the later figure gives 20.00%, the usual slip.

questions.stem_md: Finance costs of Ratnadurg Ice Factory Ltd, an imagined company, were ₹2,50,000 in 2024-25 and ₹2,00,000 in 2025-26. Its comparative statement of profit and loss shows the absolute change and the percentage change as

options.text_md: 50,000 and 20.00, an increase
(50,000) and (25.00), a decrease
(50,000) and (20.00), a decrease
50,000 and 25.00, an increase

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** (50,000) and (20.00), a decrease. Change = 2,00,000 − 2,50,000 = −50,000; −50,000 ÷ 2,50,000 × 100 = −20.00%. A fall is shown in brackets, and the base stays the earlier year.

questions.stem_md: In an inter-firm comparative statement of two imagined tile makers, with Nahargarh Tiles Ltd taken as the base firm and Mehrangarh Tiles Ltd set beside it, the percentage difference for each item is calculated on

options.text_md: the figure of Mehrangarh Tiles Ltd for that item
the total of the two firms for that item
the revenue from operations of the larger firm
the figure of Nahargarh Tiles Ltd for that item

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the figure of Nahargarh Tiles Ltd for that item. In an inter-firm statement the base firm plays the part of the earlier year: every difference is divided by its figure.

questions.stem_md: The comparative balance sheet of Kanakdurg Salt Ltd, an imagined company, shows total assets of ₹40,00,000 on 31 March 2025 and ₹46,00,000 on 31 March 2026. The change in total equity and liabilities shown in the same statement is

options.text_md: impossible to state without the list of liabilities

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹6,00,000, that is 15.00%. Both parts of a balance sheet total the same on each date, so their changes are equal in rupees and in per cent.

questions.stem_md: In the comparative statement of profit and loss of Kalinjar Stone Crafts Ltd, an imagined company, revenue from operations and total expenses both rose by 18.00%. It has no other income and the tax rate is the same in both years. Its profit after tax has therefore

options.text_md: stayed the same, because the two rises cancel out
risen by 36.00%
risen by 18.00% as well
fallen, because expenses rose

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** risen by 18.00% as well. Profit before tax is revenue minus expenses; if both grow by the same factor, so does their difference, and an unchanged tax rate carries the same growth to profit after tax.

questions.stem_md: Udayagiri Chemicals Ltd, an imagined company, held no current investments on 31 March 2025 and ₹50,000 on 31 March 2026. In its comparative balance sheet the percentage change for current investments is shown as

options.text_md: a dash: there is no earlier figure to divide by, so only the absolute change of ₹50,000 is shown
an infinitely large increase

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a dash: there is no earlier figure to divide by, so only the absolute change of ₹50,000 is shown. A percentage change needs a positive base. With a nil earlier figure the line shows the rupee change only.

questions.stem_md: Trade receivables of Rohida Rice Mills Ltd, an imagined company, rose from ₹1,60,000 to ₹1,85,000. Rounded to two decimal places, the percentage change in its comparative balance sheet is

questions.stem_md:
The managing director of Korigad Tents Ltd, an imagined company in Aambavane, tells shareholders: "Profit after tax has gone up from ₹5,00,000 to ₹6,30,000, so the company has clearly become more efficient." Revenue from operations rose from ₹40,00,000 to ₹60,00,000 over the same two years.

(a) Work out the percentage change in revenue and in profit after tax, as a comparative statement would show them. (2 marks)
(b) Work out profit after tax as a common-size percentage of revenue for both years and evaluate the managing director's claim. (3 marks)
questions.solution_md: Test the claim twice, once as a change over time and once as a share of revenue, then give a balanced verdict.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Item | 2024-25 | 2025-26 | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Revenue from operations (₹) | 40,00,000 | 60,00,000 | 50.00% |
| Profit after tax (₹) | 5,00,000 | 6,30,000 | 26.00% |
| Profit after tax as % of revenue | 12.50% | 10.50% | down 2.00 points |

**(a)** Revenue: 20,00,000 ÷ 40,00,000 × 100 = 50.00%. Profit after tax: 1,30,000 ÷ 5,00,000 × 100 = 26.00%.

**(b)** Profit after tax was 12.50% of revenue and is now 10.50%. In rupees the claim is true: profit rose by ₹1,30,000. But profit grew only about half as fast as revenue, and each rupee of sales now earns less, so costs grew faster than sales or prices were cut to win volume. The company is bigger, not more efficient: the claim is only partly true, and shareholders should ask which costs rose.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Profit as a percentage of revenue, both years
